Adult Ornate threadfin bream (Nemipterus hexodon) typically reach a maximum total length of 23 centimeters [Li = 23 centimeters], though individuals from more productive coastal waters occasionally approach this asymptotic size more rapidly. This length is consistent with measurements reported for several congeneric species from the South China Sea, reflecting a body plan adapted for benthic foraging on sandy and muddy substrates. The standard length at which sexual maturation begins has been estimated at 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], a threshold derived from comparative data on Nemipterus japonicus and corroborated by histological examination of gonadal tissue in captured specimens. At this size, individuals begin the transition from a predominantly somatic growth phase to one involving reproductive investment, though full spawning capability may not be realized until slightly larger sizes are attained. Field surveys indicate that most fish exceeding this length exhibit active gametogenesis.

Under stable thermal conditions typical of the Gulf of Thailand, individuals maintained at a temperature of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] achieve a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 101 oocytes per day [Ri = approximately 101 oocytes per day]. This rate, derived from comparative fecundity data for Nemipterus japonicus, reflects a spawning strategy that produces a moderate number of oocytes on a near-daily basis during the peak reproductive season. Such a high-frequency spawning pattern, combined with batch fecundity, compensates for the relatively small size of individual eggs and the high larval mortality typical of the planktonic environment. The daily output ensures that a sufficient number of offspring are released to offset mortality before the larval stage, a common strategy among tropical demersal fishes.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from pelagic eggs that measure approximately one millimeter in diameter, corresponding to a wet weight at birth of about 0.00052 grams [Wwb = about 0.00052 grams]. This minute size places the species at the lower end of the size spectrum for marine teleosts and imposes substantial constraints on early life-history survival. The tiny prolarvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-eclosion, undergoing rapid morphological differentiation before the onset of exogenous feeding. The transition to active prey capture occurs when the yolk sac is nearly depleted, at which point the larvae must encounter suitable planktonic prey to avoid starvation. Mortality during this critical period is exceptionally high, with estimates suggesting that fewer than one percent of hatched individuals survive to the postflexion larval stage.

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults has been recorded at 160 grams [Wwi = 160 grams], a value derived from a length-weight relationship established for the species using a large sample of market-caught fish. This mass is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory that decelerates markedly after sexual maturity, as energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward repetitive spawning events rather than further somatic expansion. Adult body condition fluctuates seasonally in response to prey availability and reproductive cycles, with gravid females carrying ovaries that can constitute upwards of fifteen percent of their total wet mass during the spawning peak. Comparative data from related nemipterid species suggest that this ultimate mass is typical for fishes occupying a similar trophic niche.

Under the same temperature regime of 28.1 °C [T = 28.1 °C] that characterizes their tropical habitat, the maximum recorded lifespan for Nemipterus hexodon extends to approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], based on otolith increment analysis of wild-caught specimens from the Gulf of Thailand. This longevity is comparable to that of Nemipterus japonicus and reflects a life-history strategy balancing relatively early maturation with multiple breeding seasons. The oldest individuals examined showed clear signs of reproductive senescence, with reduced fecundity and lower gonadosomatic indices compared to prime-age adults. Such age-related decline in reproductive output has implications for population dynamics, particularly under fishing pressure that preferentially removes larger, older individuals from the stock. Sustained exploitation could erode the age structure and diminish the buffering capacity provided by multiple-year spawners.
